title: EZEKIEL PUT THIS SEXUAL ACT ON JERUSALEM’S LIST OF COVENANT VIOLATIONS—AND ALMOST NOBODY TALKS ABOUT IT
paragraphs: EZEKIEL PUT THIS SEXUAL ACT ON JERUSALEM’S LIST OF COVENANT VIOLATIONS—AND ALMOST NOBODY TALKS ABOUT IT

Ezekiel 18:6 and 22:10 mention sexual relations during menstruation in passages about covenant faithfulness and Jerusalem’s corruption. But before turning an uncomfortable Bible passage into either a weapon or an embarrassment, we need to hear what God was actually saying—and then follow the story all the way to Jesus Christ.
There are Bible verses we underline.
There are Bible verses we quote when life hurts.
There are verses we put on coffee mugs, phone wallpapers, T-shirts, and church walls.
And then there are verses we quietly walk past.
You can read Ezekiel for years, remember the valley of dry bones, remember the watchman, remember the strange visions, remember the promise of a new heart...
In describing a righteous man, Ezekiel says:
“And he does not approach a menstruating woman.”
The context makes the sexual meaning clear.

Ezekiel is describing a man who practices righteousness. He does not participate in idolatrous worship. He does not defile his neighbor’s wife. He does not approach a woman during her menstrual impurity. He does not oppress people. He restores what he has taken in pledge. He does not rob. He feeds the hungry. He clothes the naked. He refuses unjust gain. He practices justice. He walks faithfully in God’s statutes.
“He is righteous; he shall surely live.”
Because the menstruation statement is not floating alone in Scripture as some bizarre divine obsession with a woman’s biology.
It sits inside a much larger picture of covenant faithfulness.
Ezekiel refuses to let people divide life into the “religious” things God cares about and the “private” things God supposedly ignores.
God cared about the hungry person outside your door.
God cared about what you did with money.
God cared about how you treated your neighbor.
God cared about what happened when nobody else was watching.
And that is where this uncomfortable verse suddenly becomes uncomfortable for reasons much deeper than menstruation.
Because Ezekiel is confronting one of humanity’s oldest spiritual lies:
“This part of my life belongs to me.”
My private messages belong to me.
My business practices belong to me.
My secret browser history belongs to me.
My hidden life belongs to me.
And God keeps walking into the rooms we labeled PRIVATE.
Not because He delights in humiliation.
The wording in Ezekiel deliberately echoes the Torah.
וְאֶל־אִשָּׁה בְּנִדַּת טֻמְאָתָהּ לֹא תִקְרַב לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָתָהּ
Ve’el ishshah beniddat tum’atah lo tiqrav legalot ervatah.
You shall not approach a woman during her menstrual impurity to uncover her nakedness.
That final expression removes much of the ambiguity. “Uncovering nakedness” is sexual language in this context.
Leviticus 20:18 addresses the matter again, describing a man lying with a menstruating woman and attaching a covenant sanction to the violation.
So Ezekiel did not invent a new sexual ethic.
He was calling Israel back to a covenant command Israel already possessed.
But then Ezekiel says something even darker.
Jerusalem had become so corrupt that the prophet indicts the city in Ezekiel 22.
The first half concerns uncovering a father’s nakedness—an idiom connected with illicit sexual relations involving a father’s wife.
Then comes the chilling second accusation.
Women in menstrual impurity were עִנּוּ — ʿinnû.
The verb can carry the sense of humiliating, afflicting, humbling, or violating.
That is why responsible English translations differ in exactly how forcefully they render the verse.
Ezekiel 18:6 describes the righteous man refusing the forbidden sexual approach.
Ezekiel 22:10 portrays Jerusalem’s corruption with darker language of humiliation or violation.
We should not make Scripture say less than it says.
But neither should we make it say more.
And we certainly should not turn these passages into permission to degrade women.
Menstruation itself is not presented as a moral sin committed by a woman.
A woman did not become morally wicked because her body menstruated.
The Torah contains an entire system of ritual purity and impurity, and ritual impurity must not automatically be equated with personal moral guilt.
A corpse could render someone unclean.
None of that means a dead body had sinned, childbirth was wicked, or normal biological processes made someone morally evil.
So if someone uses Ezekiel 18:6 to tell a woman that menstruation makes her disgusting to God...
And if someone uses this passage to humiliate women...
they have managed to weaponize a passage that actually places responsibility upon covenant obedience.
The Bible is not ashamed of the human body.
The scandal in Ezekiel is not that women menstruate.
The scandal is that God's covenant people repeatedly treated His boundaries as though they were suggestions.
And suddenly this ancient text is standing much closer to us than we expected.
Because maybe your specific hidden compromise is not the one Ezekiel names.
Maybe everybody at church thinks you are strong.
Maybe you know exactly when to lift your hands during worship.
Maybe you know Christian vocabulary so well that you can describe surrender without actually surrendering.
Maybe you post Scripture publicly while negotiating with sin privately.
And maybe that is why Ezekiel feels invasive.
Because God is not merely asking whether Jerusalem still had religion.
What Jerusalem increasingly lacked was covenant faithfulness.
And eventually God says something devastating in Ezekiel 22:12:
That is what sin eventually does.
It does not always begin with someone screaming, “I hate God.”
Sometimes it begins much more quietly.
You stop trembling at His Word.
You start explaining away what once convicted you.
You become more concerned with being exposed than being holy.
You learn how to live with what once made you weep.
You just stop letting Jesus enter certain rooms.
And perhaps someone reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
At least you desperately want to.
But there is something you have been hiding.
Something you cannot imagine telling another believer because you are terrified they will never look at you the same way again.
And eventually shame starts preaching its own gospel to you.
“God might forgive other people, but not this.”
“If people knew the real story, they would leave.”
But shame is a terrible theologian.
Because Ezekiel does not end with Jerusalem’s scandal.
The same prophetic book that exposes defilement also announces astonishing restoration.
God promises that the heart of stone will be removed.
And centuries later, Jesus Christ comes.
Not pretending sin does not matter.
He comes bearing something infinitely more costly.
This is where Christianity becomes unlike cheap spirituality.
God does not save us by announcing that sin was never serious.
God saves sinners at enormous cost.
The innocent One suffers for the guilty.
The Holy One gives Himself for sinners.
The One without scandal steps into ours.
And the Gospel says something shame never expected:
your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Repentance is not God asking you to pretend the wound never happened.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the God who can actually cleanse sinners.
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved.
Grace does not say, “Sin does not matter.”
Grace says, “Sin mattered enough for Christ to bleed—and you matter enough that He calls you out of it.”
That is why Jesus can look at people carrying histories that would make religious crowds whisper...
Because repentance finally has somewhere to run.
Maybe that is what you need tonight.
Not another promise that you will fix yourself next week.
You may need to close the door.
“Jesus, this is what I keep returning to.”
“Jesus, this is what happened to me.”
There is no benefit in hiding from the One who already knows.
And there is breathtaking hope in discovering that the One who already knows is the One whose hands were pierced for sinners.
If this exposed something you have kept hidden, you do not need to publish the details of your private sin for strangers.
But you can make a simple declaration of surrender.
Not because typing words saves anybody.
But sometimes a small public confession that we need Christ becomes the moment we stop protecting the mask.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to discover they are not the only believer fighting for holiness.
If you were sexually violated, coerced, abused, or assaulted, the sin committed against you is not transformed into your guilt simply because your body was involved.
Do not let somebody misuse Ezekiel 22:10 to place an offender’s guilt upon the wounded.
God sees what happened behind closed doors.
The Lord who condemns exploitation is not confused about the difference between committing evil and suffering evil at someone else's hands.
But what happened to you does not place you beyond the reach of Jesus.
Maybe that is the sentence somebody needed to survive tonight.
And maybe someone you know needs this entire message.
Your share may put it in front of them.
We do not need to hide difficult Scripture.
We need to read it carefully, faithfully, humbly, and ultimately through the redemptive story that leads us to Christ.
Because temptation has a way of making yesterday's convictions feel distant.
Shame has a way of making grace feel impossible.
And there may come a night when you need to read again that God exposes darkness not because darkness is stronger than Him...
but because He calls people into the light.
There is enough shallow Christianity online.
We want to keep opening the Bible.
And for believers who want to help Gospel Warrior continue and expand this work, there is another practical way to stand with the mission.
But I want to say this without manipulating your conscience:

Scripture explicitly teaches that Christian giving should not be extracted through compulsion. Paul says giving should come from what a person has purposed in the heart, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Keep reaching people scrolling alone at midnight who may never walk through a church door but will stop when a sentence suddenly sounds like God is calling them home.
And if you cannot financially support Gospel Warrior, please do not disappear.
A sincere share can travel farther than money sometimes can.
Because this was never supposed to be about building an audience that admires Gospel Warrior.
It is about pointing an audience toward Jesus Christ.
Ezekiel named what Jerusalem wanted to normalize.
He exposed what people wanted left in darkness.
But Scripture does not expose sin merely so sinners can stand naked beneath accusation forever.
Maybe you came into this article because the title shocked you.
Maybe you stayed because you wanted to know what Ezekiel actually meant.
But perhaps somewhere along the way the question changed.
“Why does the Bible mention sex during menstruation?”
“What part of my life have I been telling Jesus He cannot touch?”
That is the question worth carrying into prayer.
Because the God who sees Jerusalem's corruption also sees ours.
The God who named Israel's hidden violations knows every hidden thing in us.
Yet the Gospel announces that judgment does not have to be the final word for the sinner who turns to Christ.
Bring Him the thing you were praying nobody would ever discover.
And still He calls sinners to come.
Because maybe the most terrifying thing about Ezekiel is that God sees what we hide.
But maybe the most beautiful thing about the Gospel is exactly the same:
Jesus saw the chapter you were desperately trying to hide—and He still walked toward the cross to make redemption possible.
